title: Greedy Best-First in Lviv: can it find the fast way?
description: Watch Greedy Best-First navigate real street-map geometry in Lviv, choosing the next intersection by the most promising heuristic. Spoiler: it’s fast and visually satisfying—yet it may miss the absolute shortest route.
ig_caption:
🧭✨ Lviv street map time! In this reel, **Greedy Best-First** picks the next node that *looks* closest to the goal using a heuristic (usually something like straight-line distance).  

📍Graph theory view: we model intersections and roads as a **graph** (nodes + edges). Greedy Best-First maintains a priority queue ordered by **h(n)**, so it expands the most “promising” frontier node first—**ignoring the path cost so far** (g(n)).  

🧠🔥 Why it’s cool: on real maps, this heuristic-driven behavior often produces a route quickly, and the visualization makes the search frontier “snap” toward the target.  

⚠️Tradeoff: because it’s greedy, it can get pulled into locally attractive corridors and take a **non-optimal** path compared to algorithms that consider g(n) too.  

👉 Try it yourself: comment **“HEURISTIC”** and tell me what heuristic you’d use for roads (Euclidean vs. Manhattan vs. travel-time proxies). If you want, I can generate a follow-up with weighted edges + obstacles!
fb_caption:
🚦In this visualization from **Lviv (Plosha Rynok)**, we run **Greedy Best-First** over a real street-map graph. It treats intersections as nodes and roads as edges, then always expands the next node with the smallest heuristic distance to the goal (h(n)).

📌 Key idea: this is a **heuristic-driven graph search**—fast to converge visually, but it may not guarantee the shortest route because it doesn’t fully account for the cost accumulated so far.

💬 Share this with a friend who loves algorithms, and ask: should “closest-looking” always win, or should we balance exploration and path cost?
